hints: Focus on the reaction condition first, as acid hydrolysis and alkaline hydrolysis of esters give different types of products.
Remember that any carboxylic acid, $\text{R'CO}_2\text{H}$, formed in the presence of alkali like $\text{NaOH}$ will immediately be deprotonated.
Think about which fragment keeps the proton to become neutral, the acid part or the alcohol part, when $\text{OH}^-$ is present.
walkthrough:
**Recall the two types of ester hydrolysis**

Ester hydrolysis always splits the ester into its acid part and its alcohol part. Think of $\text{R'CO}_2\text{R''}$ breaking at the C-O bond.

$$\text{R'CO}_2\text{R''} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{acid fragment} + \text{alcohol fragment}$$

**Apply the alkaline condition**

In acid conditions you get the neutral molecules, $\text{R'CO}_2\text{H}$ and $\text{R''OH}$. But in alkaline conditions, $\text{OH}^-$ removes the acidic proton.

$$\text{R'CO}_2\text{H} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{R'CO}_2^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Identify the final pair**

So the acid part ends up as the carboxylate anion, $\text{R'CO}_2^-$. The alcohol part stays as the neutral alcohol, $\text{R''OH}$, because alcohols are very weak acids and are not deprotonated by dilute alkali.

options.A: This pair, $\text{R'CO}_2\text{H}$ and $\text{R''OH}$, is the result of acid hydrolysis with dilute HCl or $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$. It is the trap for forgetting that alkali will deprotonate the carboxylic acid.
options.B: Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) gives the carboxylate salt and the free alcohol. The $\text{R'CO}_2^-$ anion forms because the acid is neutralised by $\text{OH}^-$, while $\text{R''OH}$ remains neutral. Well done if you spotted this.
options.C: This gets it backwards. $\text{R''O}^-$ is an alkoxide ion, a very strong base, and it would immediately take a proton from water to give $\text{R''OH}$. Meanwhile the carboxylic acid would lose its proton, not keep it.
options.D: Both products cannot be anions in aqueous alkaline hydrolysis. While $\text{R'CO}_2^-$ is correct, $\text{R''O}^-$ is too basic to survive in water and will exist as neutral $\text{R''OH}$.
